author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Silvia, a young woman with an inherited gift for summoning vast, alien 'angels' by offering trays of lamb's blood in her family's garden, treats the ritual as a private thrill she has practiced since childhood — she believes herself descended from these beings and destined to eventually join them.
page_summary:
Silvia, a young woman with an inherited gift for summoning vast, alien 'angels' by offering trays of lamb's blood in her family's garden, treats the ritual as a private thrill she has practiced since childhood — she believes herself descended from these beings and destined to eventually join them. Her fiancé Rick disapproves but is drawn into the ritual anyway; during one summoning, Silvia cuts her finger and, before the wound can be treated, the angels seize her prematurely, incinerating her body and leaving only ash. Rick refuses to accept her death: he returns alone to the trough, pours fresh blood, and negotiates directly with the alien presences, insisting they owe Silvia a return since the mistake was theirs. They agree, but warn him the crossing is dangerous and that Silvia will need to occupy a 'clay' vessel — a living body — since her original one was destroyed. Rick insists on bringing her back regardless of the risk, and the return begins to go wrong immediately: rather than returning to one host, whatever mechanism is transferring her begins possessing every person she brushes against in sequence — her sister, then her mother, then strangers on the highway, a waitress, a hitchhiker — each one becoming Silvia for a moment before the transfer moves on, an expanding wave of identical dazed women (and briefly men) repeating her exact words and gestures, spreading outward from the house across the country and, implicitly, across the world. The story ends with Rick, exhausted, arriving home to find his own reflection wavering into Silvia's face in the bathroom mirror — the transfer finally overtaking him, the one person who caused it.

**Why it matters.** Sutin identifies this story explicitly as 'Phil's take on the Orpheus legend, with a lover seeking to rescue his Eurydice from life after death' — a classification that clarifies the story's mythic scaffolding precisely: Rick's insistence on bringing Silvia back against clear warning is the same fatal impatience that dooms Orpheus's rescue, transposed into a cosmic-horror register where the consequence of failure is not merely losing her again but an uncontrolled, world-spanning identity collapse. What distinguishes this story from a simple myth-retelling is its ending: Orpheus loses only Eurydice a second time, but Rick loses the entire distinction between self and other, ending the story staring at his own face becoming hers — the myth's personal tragedy escalated into an ontological one that implicates the reader's world along with the character's.

*Rick's own reflection in the bathroom mirror begins to waver into Silvia's face in the story's last lines — the transfer that began with his refusal to accept her death now claims the one person whose love caused it.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: the ritual and its fatal accident, the negotiated return, the uncontrolled spreading transfer
movements: The blood ritual, Silvia's belief in her angelic ancestry, and her death when the summoned beings take her before the wound can be treated.
Rick's confrontation with the alien presences and his insistence, against their explicit warning, that they return her to Earth.
The transfer spreading uncontrollably from host to host — sister, mother, strangers, a whole town, then a whole country — ending with Rick himself overtaken in his own mirror.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Rick throughout, tracking his descent from grief and demand into horrified witness of a catastrophe entirely of his own making, which finally consumes him too.
structure.central_device: Love and refusal-to-accept-loss as the actual mechanism of catastrophe — Rick's insistence on getting Silvia back, over the beings' explicit warning that the crossing is unstable, is what triggers an escalating, unstoppable identity-replication that ultimately erases the distinction between Silvia and everyone else, including him.

characters.name: Silvia Everett
characters.role: the summoner, later the spreading transferred identity
characters.note: Describes her own eventual death and ascension in the imagery of metamorphosis rather than loss — 'we won't be worms any more' — and the story never fully resolves whether her death was truly premature or simply what she had always wanted.

characters.name: Rick
characters.note: His love for Silvia is genuine and his refusal to accept her death is sympathetic, which is exactly what makes his insistence on forcing her return, against explicit warning, a tragedy of good intention rather than villainy.

characters.name: Walter Everett
characters.note: Has watched this coming his whole life — 'They're flies, hovering around, waiting for you' — and is proven right in a way worse than he expected.

characters.name: The winged beings
characters.note: Not cruel by disposition — they acknowledge their own mistake in taking Silvia prematurely and attempt to correct it exactly as asked, and the catastrophe that follows is a direct, honestly-warned-of consequence of Rick's own choice rather than any deception on their part.

settings.name: The Everett family garden
settings.note: An ordinary suburban garden — roses, cedars, a sundial — that doubles as a threshold to another order of reality, entirely through the family's private ritual.

settings.name: The open road
settings.note: Where the transfer's uncontrolled spread becomes visible and cinematic — identical women appearing at gas stations, diners, and eventually across entire nations, the horror scaling from domestic to planetary within a single drive.

motifs: Blood as the literal medium of contact between the human and the alien/divine, echoing Homeric and Christian precedent the characters cite directly (Ulysses' trench, martyrs' blood)
A being who is not truly her own physical form on the far side, requiring a 'clay' vessel to return — the story's most explicit statement of its Genesis allusion
An identity-transfer that will not stay contained to a single host, replicating outward with no apparent limit
Ordinary strangers (a waitress, a hitchhiker, a traffic cop) becoming interchangeable vessels for the same voice and face
A protagonist's love and refusal of loss as the direct cause of a catastrophe he cannot undo or outrun

distinctive_terms.label: Garden
distinctive_terms.note: The site of the summoning ritual, and an implicit Eden allusion given the story's explicit references to a Creator shaping 'clay.'

distinctive_terms.label: Gods
distinctive_terms.note: Silvia's own word for what she and the winged beings will become — 'transfiguration — from clay into gods.'

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick's letters confirm the story's inclusion in The Best of Philip K. Dick and his own preference for its title over an alternative.

evidence.quote: The only reason I can see for not going ahead with this would be if it were to conflict with other sales of "Upon the Dull Earth," as for instance in the BEST OF PHILIP K. DICK which Ballantine is going to bring out.
evidence.reading: Confirms the story's inclusion in the major 1977 retrospective collection, and Dick's own attentiveness to rights conflicts around it.

evidence.quote: "Oh, To Be a Blobel." "Roog." "Upon the Dull Earth." Personally, although Don Wollheim used "Breakfast At Twilight," I'd like to see it included, with "The De[fenders]
evidence.reading: Dick discussing anthology contents and expressing a specific preference for including this story, in a letter also referencing 'Roog' and 'The Defenders' (both read in this project).

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: the haunting "Upon the Dull Earth" (w. 1953, p. 1954), Phil's take on the Orpheus legend, with a lover seeking to rescue his Eurydice from life after death
evidence.reading: The single most useful critical sentence found for this story: identifying its precise mythic source (Orpheus and Eurydice) and the specific way Dick's version escalates the myth's stakes.

open_questions: Sutin pairs this story with 'The Cookie Lady' as the only two fantasy pieces accepted by a particular editorial standard (R&C) — worth identifying that collection precisely.

The story's ending (Rick's own reflection becoming Silvia) is ambiguous about the ultimate scope of the catastrophe — does the transfer stabilize once it reaches him, or does the implication remain that it continues indefinitely? Worth checking whether Dick commented on the ending's intended finality anywhere.

Given the direct Orpheus/Eurydice framing, is there a deliberate echo of the myth's prohibition (not looking back) anywhere in the text that this reading may have under-weighted — Rick never explicitly 'looks back,' but his repeated recognition and pursuit of Silvia's dispersed identity across strangers may function as a structural equivalent.

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

later_use: Adapted for the anthology TV series Electric Dreams (2017).
